title: Mythology: Greek and Roman Gods and Myths
description: For beginners exploring Greek and Roman deities, heroes, monsters, and major stories. Mythic traditions vary; these original summaries identify common versions and distinguish Greek and Roman names.

sources.name: Original summaries of classical myths and ancient literary traditions

cards.front: Who is Zeus in Greek mythology?
cards.back: The ruler of the Olympian gods, associated with the sky, thunder, oaths, and kingship.

cards.front: Which Roman god is most closely identified with Zeus?
cards.back: Jupiter, also called Jove.

cards.front: Who is Hera in Greek mythology?
cards.back: The queen of the Olympian gods, wife of Zeus, and a goddess especially associated with marriage.

cards.front: Which Roman goddess is most closely identified with Hera?
cards.back: Juno.

cards.front: Who is Poseidon in Greek mythology?
cards.back: A god of the sea, earthquakes, and horses, and a brother of Zeus and Hades.

cards.front: Which Roman god is most closely identified with Poseidon?
cards.back: Neptune.

cards.front: Who is Hades in Greek mythology?
cards.back: The ruler of the underworld and a brother of Zeus and Poseidon; his name can also refer to his realm.

cards.front: Which Roman underworld god is commonly identified with Hades?
cards.back: Pluto, also associated with Dis Pater in Roman tradition.

cards.front: Who is Demeter in Greek mythology?
cards.back: A goddess of grain, agriculture, and the earth's fertility, and the mother of Persephone.

cards.front: Which Roman goddess is most closely identified with Demeter?
cards.back: Ceres.

cards.front: Who is Hestia in Greek mythology?
cards.back: The goddess of the hearth and the household's sacred fire.

cards.front: Which Roman goddess is most closely identified with Hestia?
cards.back: Vesta.

cards.front: Who is Athena in Greek mythology?
cards.back: A goddess of wisdom, crafts, and strategic warfare, and the protector of Athens.

cards.front: Which Roman goddess is most closely identified with Athena?
cards.back: Minerva.

cards.front: Who is Apollo in Greek mythology?
cards.back: A god associated with prophecy, music, archery, healing, and plague; later traditions also strongly associate him with the sun.

cards.front: What name did the Romans commonly use for Apollo?
cards.back: Apollo; unlike many Greek gods, he generally retained the same name in Roman worship.

cards.front: Who is Artemis in Greek mythology?
cards.back: A goddess of hunting, wild animals, and young people, and the twin sister of Apollo.

cards.front: Which Roman goddess is most closely identified with Artemis?
cards.back: Diana.

cards.front: Who is Ares in Greek mythology?
cards.back: A god of war, especially its violence and battle fury.

cards.front: Which Roman god is most closely identified with Ares?
cards.back: Mars, who had a broader and especially important civic role in Roman religion.

cards.front: Who is Aphrodite in Greek mythology?
cards.back: A goddess of love, beauty, and sexual desire.

cards.front: Which Roman goddess is most closely identified with Aphrodite?
cards.back: Venus.

cards.front: Who is Hephaestus in Greek mythology?
cards.back: The divine smith, associated with metalworking, craftsmanship, and fire.

cards.front: Which Roman god is most closely identified with Hephaestus?
cards.back: Vulcan.

cards.front: Who is Hermes in Greek mythology?
cards.back: A messenger god associated with travelers, trade, cunning, boundaries, and guiding souls to the underworld.

cards.front: Which Roman god is most closely identified with Hermes?
cards.back: Mercury.

cards.front: Who is Dionysus in Greek mythology?
cards.back: A god of wine, ecstatic experience, and theater.

cards.front: What Roman name is commonly used for Dionysus?
cards.back: Bacchus; Roman traditions also associated him with Liber.

cards.front: Who is Persephone in Greek mythology?
cards.back: The daughter of Demeter and queen of the underworld as the wife of Hades.

cards.front: Which Roman goddess is most closely identified with Persephone?
cards.back: Proserpina.

cards.front: Who is Eros in Greek mythology?
cards.back: A deity of love and desire; some traditions make him a primordial power, while others make him a child of Aphrodite.

cards.front: Which Roman deity is commonly identified with Eros?
cards.back: Cupid, also called Amor.

cards.front: Who is Nike in Greek mythology?
cards.back: The personification and goddess of victory.

cards.front: Which Roman goddess corresponds to Nike?
cards.back: Victoria.

cards.front: Who is Helios in Greek mythology?
cards.back: The sun god, often depicted driving the sun's chariot across the sky.

cards.front: Who is Selene in Greek mythology?
cards.back: The goddess and personification of the moon.

cards.front: Who is Eos in Greek mythology?
cards.back: The goddess and personification of dawn.

cards.front: Which Roman goddess corresponds to Eos?
cards.back: Aurora.

cards.front: Who is Pan in Greek mythology?
cards.back: A rustic god associated with shepherds, flocks, wild places, and reed pipes, often shown with goat legs and horns.

cards.front: Who is Asclepius in Greek mythology?
cards.back: A healing figure worshipped as a god of medicine, commonly associated with a staff bearing one snake.

cards.front: What is the difference between Asclepius's staff and Hermes's caduceus?
cards.back: Asclepius's staff bears one snake; Hermes's caduceus typically bears two snakes and often wings.

cards.front: Who is Hecate in Greek mythology?
cards.back: A goddess associated with crossroads, torches, magic, and the night in many later traditions.

cards.front: Who is Gaia in Greek mythology?
cards.back: The personified Earth, a primordial deity and mother of many early divine beings.

cards.front: Who is Uranus in Greek mythology?
cards.back: The personified sky, partner of Gaia and father of the Titans in Hesiod's account.

cards.front: Who are the Titans?
cards.back: An older generation of divine beings, including Cronus and Rhea, who precede the Olympian order.

cards.front: Who is Cronus in Greek mythology?
cards.back: A Titan who overthrows his father Uranus and is later overthrown by his son Zeus.

cards.front: Which Roman god was identified with Cronus?
cards.back: Saturn. The identification links distinct Greek and Roman traditions rather than making every story identical.

cards.front: Who is Rhea in Greek mythology?
cards.back: A Titan and the mother of Zeus, Hera, Poseidon, Hades, Demeter, and Hestia by Cronus.

cards.front: Why does Cronus swallow his children in the familiar myth?
cards.back: He fears a prediction that one of his children will overthrow him.

cards.front: How does Rhea save the infant Zeus from Cronus?
cards.back: She hides Zeus and gives Cronus a stone wrapped in swaddling clothes to swallow instead.

cards.front: What is the Titanomachy?
cards.back: The war in which Zeus and his allies defeat the Titans and establish the Olympian order.

cards.front: What is the Gigantomachy?
cards.back: The battle between the Olympian gods and the Giants; it is distinct from the war against the Titans.

cards.front: Who is Atlas in Greek mythology?
cards.back: A Titan condemned to hold up the heavens; he does not originally carry the planet Earth on his shoulders.

cards.front: Who is Prometheus in Greek mythology?
cards.back: A Titan associated with aiding humanity, especially by obtaining fire for humans.

cards.front: How is Prometheus punished for defying Zeus in a famous tradition?
cards.back: He is bound while an eagle eats his regenerating liver until Heracles eventually frees him.

cards.front: Who is Epimetheus in Greek mythology?
cards.back: Prometheus's brother, associated with afterthought and with accepting Pandora.

cards.front: What does Pandora open in the older Greek account of her story?
cards.back: A large jar, commonly retold as a box, releasing afflictions into the human world.

cards.front: What remains in Pandora's jar in Hesiod's account?
cards.back: Elpis, usually translated as hope; its significance has been interpreted in different ways.

cards.front: Who are the Moirai, or Fates, in Greek mythology?
cards.back: Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos, who are associated with spinning, allotting, and cutting the thread of life.

cards.front: Who are the Muses?
cards.back: Goddesses who inspire poetry, music, and other arts and learning; the familiar later tradition numbers them at nine.

cards.front: Who is Mnemosyne in Greek mythology?
cards.back: The Titan associated with memory and, by Zeus, the mother of the Muses in the familiar tradition.

cards.front: Who are the Erinyes, also called the Furies?
cards.back: Divine avengers of grave wrongs, especially offenses against family bonds and oaths.

cards.front: Who is Charon in Greek mythology?
cards.back: The ferryman who carries the dead across an underworld river in familiar accounts.

cards.front: Who is Cerberus in Greek mythology?
cards.back: The monstrous hound guarding the entrance to the underworld, commonly depicted with three heads.

cards.front: What is the River Styx associated with in Greek myth?
cards.back: The underworld and solemn divine oaths; it is one of the rivers linked to the realm of the dead.

cards.front: What is Lethe in Greek mythology?
cards.back: An underworld river associated with forgetfulness.

cards.front: What is Tartarus in Greek mythology?
cards.back: A deep region of the cosmos associated with confinement and punishment; it is also personified as a primordial being.

cards.front: What is Elysium in Greek mythology?
cards.back: A blessed realm or afterlife destination for favored figures, with eligibility varying across traditions.

cards.front: Why does Persephone spend part of the year in the underworld?
cards.back: In familiar versions, eating pomegranate seeds binds her to return there for part of the year; the precise division varies.

cards.front: How is Demeter's grief connected to the seasons in the Persephone myth?
cards.back: Her separation from Persephone is associated with the earth's loss of fertility, while their reunion restores growth.

cards.front: Who is Heracles in Greek mythology?
cards.back: A heroic son of Zeus and Alcmene, celebrated for extraordinary strength and the Twelve Labors.

cards.front: What is the Roman name of Heracles?
cards.back: Hercules.

cards.front: Who assigns Heracles his famous labors?
cards.back: King Eurystheus.

cards.front: What is Heracles's first labor in the usual sequence?
cards.back: Killing the Nemean Lion, whose hide resists ordinary weapons.

cards.front: How does Heracles defeat the Lernaean Hydra with Iolaus's help?
cards.back: Heracles cuts off its heads while Iolaus cauterizes the necks to prevent new heads from growing, in the familiar account.

cards.front: How does Heracles clean the Augean stables?
cards.back: By diverting rivers so their water washes through the stables.

cards.front: What creature does Heracles bring from the underworld as a labor?
cards.back: Cerberus, the underworld's guardian hound.

cards.front: Who is Perseus in Greek mythology?
cards.back: A hero, son of Zeus and Danaë, famous for killing Medusa and rescuing Andromeda.

cards.front: Who is Medusa in Greek mythology?
cards.back: One of the Gorgons, whose gaze turns observers to stone in the familiar story; Perseus beheads her.

cards.front: How does Perseus avoid looking directly at Medusa in a familiar version?
cards.back: He uses a reflective shield to see her indirectly.

cards.front: Who is Andromeda in Greek mythology?
cards.back: A princess exposed to a sea monster and rescued by Perseus, whom she marries.

cards.front: Who is Pegasus in Greek mythology?
cards.back: A winged horse, commonly said to spring from Medusa after her beheading.

cards.front: Who is Bellerophon in Greek mythology?
cards.back: The hero who rides Pegasus and kills the Chimera.

cards.front: What is the Chimera in Greek mythology?
cards.back: A fire-breathing monster combining lion, goat, and serpent features.

cards.front: Who is Theseus in Greek mythology?
cards.back: An Athenian hero especially known for entering the Labyrinth and killing the Minotaur.

cards.front: What is the Minotaur?
cards.back: A monster with a bull's head and human body, confined in the Labyrinth on Crete.

cards.front: Who helps Theseus find his way out of the Labyrinth?
cards.back: Ariadne, who gives him a thread to trace his path in the familiar account.

cards.front: Who builds the Labyrinth in Greek mythology?
cards.back: Daedalus, the ingenious craftsman.

cards.front: Why does Icarus fall during his escape with Daedalus?
cards.back: He flies too near the sun, causing the wax in his artificial wings to soften and the wings to fail.

cards.front: Who leads the Argonauts in their quest?
cards.back: Jason.

cards.front: What object do Jason and the Argonauts seek?
cards.back: The Golden Fleece, kept in Colchis.

cards.front: Who helps Jason obtain the Golden Fleece?
cards.back: Medea, daughter of King Aeëtes of Colchis, who uses her knowledge and magic to aid him.

cards.front: Who is Orpheus in Greek mythology?
cards.back: A legendary singer and musician whose music charms living creatures and even powers of the underworld.

cards.front: Why does Orpheus lose Eurydice again after gaining permission to lead her out?
cards.back: He looks back before completing the required journey out of the underworld, violating the condition of her release.

cards.front: Who is Sisyphus in Greek mythology?
cards.back: A cunning king punished in the underworld by repeatedly pushing a stone uphill only for it to roll down again.

cards.front: What is Tantalus's famous punishment?
cards.back: He stands near food and water that continually withdraw when he tries to eat or drink.

cards.front: What is Midas's golden touch?
cards.back: A gift that turns what he touches to gold, becoming disastrous when food and drink are transformed too.

cards.front: Who is Narcissus in Greek mythology?
cards.back: A beautiful youth who becomes consumed by desire for his own reflection.

cards.front: Who is Echo in the familiar myth of Echo and Narcissus?
cards.back: A nymph restricted to repeating others' words, who loves Narcissus without being loved in return.

cards.front: What happens to Daphne as she flees Apollo in the familiar myth?
cards.back: She is transformed into a laurel tree.

cards.front: What is Arachne's contest with Athena about?
cards.back: Weaving; the story ends with Arachne transformed into a spider.

cards.front: What is the Judgment of Paris?
cards.back: Paris chooses Aphrodite over Hera and Athena in a divine beauty contest, after being offered Helen as a reward.

cards.front: Who is Helen's husband before her departure for Troy?
cards.back: Menelaus, king of Sparta.

cards.front: Who commands the Greek expedition against Troy in the Iliad's setting?
cards.back: Agamemnon, king of Mycenae and brother of Menelaus.

cards.front: Who is Achilles in Greek mythology?
cards.back: The leading Greek warrior in the Trojan War tradition, son of Peleus and the sea goddess Thetis.

cards.front: What is the central quarrel opening the Iliad?
cards.back: Achilles clashes with Agamemnon over honor and the captive woman Briseis, then withdraws from battle.

cards.front: Whose death brings Achilles back into battle in the Iliad?
cards.back: The death of Patroclus, killed by Hector.

cards.front: Who is Hector in the Iliad?
cards.back: Troy's leading defender, son of King Priam and husband of Andromache.

cards.front: Who comes to Achilles to request Hector's body?
cards.back: Priam, Hector's father and king of Troy.

cards.front: Does the Iliad narrate the fall of Troy itself?
cards.back: No. It ends with Hector's funeral; the city's fall is told in other works and traditions.

cards.front: What is the Trojan Horse stratagem?
cards.back: Greek warriors hide inside a large wooden horse brought into Troy, enabling the city's capture.

cards.front: Who is Odysseus in Greek mythology?
cards.back: The resourceful king of Ithaca, a Greek leader at Troy and the central hero of the Odyssey.

cards.front: What is a common Roman name for Odysseus?
cards.back: Ulysses.

cards.front: Who are Penelope and Telemachus in the Odyssey?
cards.back: Penelope is Odysseus's wife; Telemachus is their son.

cards.front: How does Odysseus deceive Polyphemus about his identity?
cards.back: He calls himself Nobody, so the Cyclops's cry that Nobody is hurting him fails to summon effective help.

cards.front: How does Odysseus hear the Sirens without steering toward them?
cards.back: His crew plug their own ears with wax and bind him to the mast, under instructions not to release him.

cards.front: Who is Aeneas in Greco-Roman mythology?
cards.back: A Trojan hero, son of Aphrodite or Venus and Anchises, whose journey to Italy is central to Virgil's Aeneid.

cards.front: Who is Dido in the Aeneid?
cards.back: The queen of Carthage who loves Aeneas and dies after he departs to pursue his destiny in Italy.

cards.front: Who are Romulus and Remus in Roman foundation legend?
cards.back: Twin brothers, traditionally sons of Mars and Rhea Silvia, raised after being suckled by a she-wolf; Romulus becomes Rome's founder.

cards.front: Who is Janus in Roman religion and mythology?
cards.back: A god of beginnings, transitions, doorways, and passages, commonly depicted with two faces.
